title: HANAFI RULINGS
entries: Obligatory. In Hanafi law, a fard duty is established by decisive evidence; deliberately leaving it is sinful.
Required in Hanafi law, but established by evidence that is less decisive than fard. Deliberately leaving it is sinful.
An emphasized Sunnah that the Prophet regularly practiced. Habitually neglecting it without excuse is blameworthy.
A practice taught or modeled by the Prophet. Following it is rewarded.
Recommended. Doing it is rewarded; leaving it is not sinful.
Permitted or neutral. The act is allowed in itself.
Mildly disliked. Avoiding it is better and rewarded; doing it is not treated like a prohibited act.
Prohibitively disliked in Hanafi law. It must be avoided and deliberately doing it is sinful.
Forbidden. Deliberately doing it is sinful.

title: PURIFICATION TERMS
entries: Purity or purification, including ritual purity and removal of physical impurity.
The minor ritual washing required for salah and certain other acts of worship.
A full ritual bath required after major ritual impurity and in certain other situations.
Dry purification using clean earth or a qualifying earth-like substance when water cannot be used.
Physical impurity, such as urine or blood, that must be removed when required for worship.
A state of ritual impurity that requires wudu or ghusl. It is not the same thing as physical dirt.
An excused person under Hanafi law whose chronic condition continuously causes something that would normally break wudu.
Cleaning the private areas after using the toilet.
Wiping with wet hands, such as wiping part of the head during wudu.

title: SALAH TERMS
entries: One complete unit of salah, containing its prescribed standing, recitation, bowing, prostrations, and other actions.
Recitation, especially recitation of the Qur’an in salah.
Saying “Allahu Akbar.” The opening takbir begins the prayer.
Prostration in salah, with the forehead and nose placed on the ground along with the required limbs.
The testimony recited while sitting in salah, beginning with al-Tahiyyat.
The greeting that ends the prayer, turning to the right and left.

title: PEOPLE & PRACTICE
entries: The person leading the congregational prayer.
A person praying behind and following an imam.
A latecomer who joins the imam after missing part of the congregational prayer.
The call announcing that the time for an obligatory prayer has entered.
The second call given immediately before the congregational obligatory prayer begins.
The person who gives the adhan.
The direction of the Ka‘bah in Makkah, toward which Muslims face in salah.
Intention in the heart to perform an act of worship.
A formal sermon, such as the sermon delivered before the Jumu‘ah prayer.

title: HANAFI STUDY WORDS
entries: The understanding and study of practical Islamic rulings and how they apply.
A disciplined school and method of Islamic law. The Hanafi madhhab is one of the four major Sunni schools.
Relating to the school of Islamic law associated with Imam Abu Hanifa and developed by his students and later jurists.
A legal answer or opinion given by a qualified scholar in response to a religious question.
A qualified scholar who gives fatwas.
Qualified scholarly effort used to derive or determine a ruling from the Islamic sources.
Legal analogy: applying a known ruling to a new case because they share a legally relevant cause.
Scholarly consensus. It is one of the recognized sources used in Islamic legal reasoning.
The principles and methods used to understand the legal sources and derive rulings from them.

title: COMMON ISLAMIC TERMS
entries: Supplication: directly asking Allah for help, forgiveness, guidance, or any good.
Remembrance of Allah through words, recitation, praise, and other acts of remembrance.
Repentance: turning back to Allah, leaving the sin, regretting it, and sincerely intending not to return to it.
Consciousness of Allah that leads a person to obey Him and guard against sin.
Voluntary charity given for the sake of Allah.
Obligatory charity due on qualifying wealth when its conditions are met.
The minimum qualifying amount of wealth used in determining whether zakat is due.
Voluntary worship beyond what is obligatory or required.
